meta.title: Navajo B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 307 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Navajo → English (see the Navajo, recall the meaning) and English → Navajo (see an English meaning, recall the Navajo). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 307 words for a learner who has finished A2, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on topics that are familiar or of personal interest, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Navajo (Diné bizaad), so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. All 307 of its words come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — knowledge and opinions, belief and ceremony, government, law and society, work, money and trade, family and life events, health, feelings and character, the land and the environment, food and drink, the modern world, describing words, and the verbs, adverbs and small words of connected speech — chosen from English Wiktionary's Navajo entries, since the levels below already teach every word that both the Navajo Wikipedia and Wiktionary's own example sentences use. The cards are dealt by those two counts where a word has one, and the rest follow. Every headword is printed in the standard Navajo spelling, which writes what English spelling has no letter for: a high tone with an acute accent (á), a nasal vowel with a hook (ą), a long vowel doubled (aa), the glottal stop as ʼ, and ł for the sound of Welsh ll. 199 of the 307 words also show their pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, where English Wiktionary gives it. A verb is given as Navajo dictionaries cite it, in the third person ('he/she is eating it'), with its 'I' and 'you' forms where the source has them; a noun for a relative or a part of the body is always somebody's in Navajo, and the card prints it as 'my …' and 'his/her …' (shimá, bimá 'mother'). Real example sentences come with 171 of the 307 words, three apiece for 41 of them, with the word picked out in colour; they are English Wiktionary's own usage examples and, for a few, Tatoeba's. There is no read-aloud button: no device carries a Navajo voice, and one without it reads the word in English. The Navajo Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters and sounds. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, pronunciation and most example sentences: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Navajo Wikipedia (dump of 2026-11-01, CC BY-SA 4.0) and Wiktionary's examples. A few sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
